articles.title: Estonia to Close Russian Border Crossings After Arson Attack
paragraphs: Estonia plans to close its road border crossings with Russia from December 1, after accusing Moscow of ordering an arson attack on a local drone maker. Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna said on Sunday that Russia's military intelligence service, the GRU, was behind the fire at Threod Systems, which was started in the early hours of Saturday.

Authorities said the attack did not cause serious damage, and eight people have been detained. Estonia shares a border of 294 kilometers with Russia. Mr. Tsahkna argued that closing the crossings would reduce Moscow's ability to carry out hostile activities and make it harder to get around sanctions. He said he had already told his counterparts in Finland, Lithuania and Latvia about the decision.

Prime Minister Kristen Michal described the incident as part of a wider "hybrid war" against Europe and said his country would not be intimidated. Russia's foreign ministry said it would study the plan and called a closure aggressive "Russophobia," but it did not respond directly to the accusation. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Estonia was building walls, and that walls have rarely helped the people who build them.

The case follows a pattern. Estonia has repeatedly warned of sabotage against NATO members that support Ukraine since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022. In mid-August, another arson attack hit Milrem Robotics, a defense company that supplies Ukraine with unmanned military vehicles. Estonian officials blamed Russia, which denied it. In September, Danish intelligence also warned of a low but growing risk of isolated strikes on infrastructure that is important to Ukraine's defense.
Hybrid war is a term for a mix of tactics, such as cyberattacks, sabotage and disinformation, that stay below the level of open warfare.

articles.title: China's Economy Loses Momentum as Exports Boom
paragraphs: China's economy lost more momentum in October, according to official data released on Monday. Retail sales rose just 0.4 percent from a year earlier, below the 0.8 percent that economists had expected and down from 1.1 percent in September. Industrial output grew 4.8 percent, also short of the forecast of 5.3 percent.

The weakest figure was investment, which fell 8.1 percent in the first ten months of the year. Analysts had predicted a decline of 7 percent. Here, investment means spending on property and infrastructure, such as housing and roads. The property downturn, now in its fifth year, has reduced household wealth and made many families cautious about spending. The unemployment rate eased to 5.1 percent, but joblessness among young people, excluding students, was close to a one-year high at 18 percent in September.

Consumer prices rose only 0.7 percent in October, a slower pace than in the previous month. By contrast, exports jumped 35.2 percent, helped by strong global demand for equipment and technology linked to artificial intelligence. China is on course to beat last year's record trade surplus of 1.2 trillion dollars, having passed 1 trillion dollars by October, the fastest it has ever done so.

Analysts say this uneven growth leaves the economy exposed to shocks from abroad. Goldman Sachs expects growth of 4.6 percent this year and 4.5 percent in 2027, citing weak domestic demand. Citi Research warned that new trade restrictions from the European Union are a major risk for exports next year, and said Beijing may offer practical concessions. Third-quarter growth was 4.5 percent, a rebound from three-year lows, but the latest figures suggest that the recovery depends heavily on customers overseas.

articles.title: Taiwan Slips to 13th in Global Digital and AI Ranking
paragraphs: Taiwan slipped one place to 13th out of 70 economies in the World Digital and AI Ranking 2026, published on November 11 by the Switzerland-based institute IMD. With a score of 92.44, the island trailed Hong Kong and Ireland, while the United States, Singapore and the Netherlands led the table. Taiwan had placed 12th in the previous edition.

The comparison with earlier editions should be treated with caution, since IMD rebuilt its methodology this year to gauge how well countries and companies can deploy artificial intelligence productively, govern it responsibly and earn public trust. The exercise draws on five factors, 15 sub-factors and 88 indicators.

Taiwan's profile is strikingly uneven. It ranked eighth for technology and infrastructure, sixth for efficiency and tenth for values, buoyed by first place in the market capitalization of IT and media stocks and second place in total research spending. Its companies also won plaudits for their agility and for their grasp of AI-related cybersecurity risks. Workforce development was a middling 16th, although Taiwan placed second for education and training.

Governance proved the Achilles' heel. Taiwan came 28th in that category and a dismal 62nd on the core government index, which measures public leadership. It also lagged behind its peers in telecommunications investment, at 49th, and in attracting highly skilled foreign personnel, also at 49th, while placing 58th for female researchers.

The Ministry of Digital Affairs said the report affirmed Taiwan's strengths in digital development, and pledged to bolster cross-agency defenses against AI-related fraud, expand research into software and generative AI, and shore up critical infrastructure and public services. Whether such measures can narrow the gap in governance remains to be seen.
